summary: This informational RFC analyzes whether Loop-Free Alternates, a method of IP fast reroute, work in service provider core and access networks. It covers link and node failures and gives guidance for topologies, especially the access network.

plainLanguage.summary: A Loop-Free Alternate is a precomputed backup next hop that can keep traffic moving after a link fails. RFC 6571 analyzes where this approach works in service-provider networks and where operators must assess their own topology.

subtitle: An analysis of Loop-Free Alternate coverage in service-provider access and core networks.

tldr.problem: Service providers need to know whether precomputed Loop-Free Alternates can protect their routes from link or node failures in their network topologies.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC analyzes four common access topologies and simulates LFA coverage in eleven service-provider core topologies, including link and node protection and transient-loop cases.
tldr.outcome: The analyzed access designs generally have strong LFA coverage, while core coverage varies substantially and calls for case-by-case analysis. The document is Informational guidance, not a routing protocol specification.

today: RFC 6571 is an Informational RFC published in June 2012. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the document analyzes the applicability of LFAs specified in RFC 5286.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 6571 analyzes the applicability of Loop-Free Alternates (LFAs), a method of IP fast reroute, in service-provider access and core networks. It considers both link and node failures and gives particular attention to access topologies.

The analysis uses IS-IS as a reference and states that it also applies to OSPF. It assumes normal routing uses shortest paths and that the links being protected are point-to-point.
sections.plainLanguage: An LFA is a backup next hop prepared before a failure happens. This RFC examines whether those backups are available in common service-provider network designs.

sections.title: Link and Node Protection
sections.content:
A per-prefix LFA is a precomputed backup next hop for one destination. A link-protecting LFA satisfies the distance condition ND < NS + SD. A node-protecting LFA must also satisfy ND < NF + FD, where F is the initial next hop.

A per-link LFA uses one backup next hop for every destination reached through a particular link. The RFC also describes de facto node protection, where multiple LFAs together keep traffic away from a failed node even though an individual LFA was not explicitly selected as node-protecting. A micro-loop is a temporary forwarding loop during routing convergence.
sections.plainLanguage: A safe backup path must avoid sending traffic back through the failed link or node. The RFC defines distance tests for checking whether an alternate protects a link, a node, or both.

sections.title: Four Access-Network Topologies
sections.content:
The RFC analyzes triangle, full-mesh, square, and extended-U access designs. These are repeated patterns in which access routers connect through aggregation routers to two routers leading toward the core. The analysis checks link and node failures and evaluates both per-prefix and per-link LFAs.

In the analyzed cases, intra-area link protection is full for the triangle, full mesh, and extended U; the square has one exception where C1 has no LFA for destination A1. Intra-area node protection is available in all four topologies. Inter-area link protection is full in the summarized cases, while node protection depends on topology and metric conditions such as e < c.
sections.plainLanguage: The four access layouts usually provide backup paths for failures inside the access area. Protection for destinations beyond that area depends on the layout and on how link costs are assigned.

sections.title: Metric Choices and Micro-Loops
sections.content:
A dual-plane core makes the metric difference e equal to zero in the described design, improving node-protection coverage. A two-tiered IGP metric plan can ensure relationships including c < a, e < c, and e < a. These conditions improve LFA coverage for inter-area destinations.

The RFC identifies a micro-loop case in the square topology: traffic to A1 may loop temporarily when link C1A1 fails and C1 updates its forwarding state before C2. The other analyzed transitions do not have micro-loop potential under the stated analysis. The extended-U topology avoids this case if its stated metric condition holds.
sections.plainLanguage: Careful link-cost choices can improve the number of destinations with safe backups. Operators must also check that routers updating at different times will not temporarily send packets in a loop.

sections.title: Core-Network Coverage Results
sections.content:
The RFC simulates eleven real service-provider core topologies, ranging from 16 to 600 nodes. Per-prefix LFA coverage ranges from 67% to 99%, with an average of 89% and a median of 94%. Per-link coverage ranges from 16% to 98%, with an average of 67% and a median of 68%.

Coverage varies widely among topologies, so the RFC recommends case-by-case analysis for core networks. It notes that per-prefix LFAs outperform per-link LFAs in the analyzed backbone set. A network may use LFAs in the access network and MPLS Traffic Engineering fast reroute in the core.
sections.plainLanguage: Core networks differ: some have backup routes for nearly every destination, while others have much lower coverage. Operators should measure their own topology rather than assume one result applies to every core.

sections.title: Operational Benefits and Planning
sections.content:
LFA is integrated with the IGP and requires no protocol change or network-wide upgrade, so it can be enabled router by router. Backup paths are computed and installed before failure. The RFC says repair under 50 milliseconds is achievable when forwarding-table updates are fast enough for the number of destinations involved.

The RFC recommends capacity-planning tools that estimate coverage, include traffic demands, test failure scenarios, and calculate load while repairs are active. LFA is not intended to replace MPLS TE fast reroute in every case. The applicable security considerations are those in RFC 5286; RFC 6571 adds none.
sections.plainLanguage: LFA is relatively simple to deploy because it is part of the existing routing process and needs no protocol change. Planning tools can show where backup coverage is missing and whether rerouted traffic would overload a link.
